newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: U.N. drawn into rivalry between Cambodia premiers.
newsitem.headline: U.N. drawn into rivalry between Cambodia premiers.

text.p: Cambodian co-Premier Prince Norodom Ranariddh said on Thursday he wanted a senior U.N. diplomat replaced in the latest crisis to shake the country's troubled coalition government.

In a letter to U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan dated April 22 and released on Thursday, Ranariddh said his coalition partner and co-Premier Hun Sen had earlier in the month requested the extension of the U.N. chief's special representative in Cambodia "without my knowledge".

"I very much welcome the nomination by the United Nations of a new Special Representative in Cambodia at the expiration of... Mr. Benny Widyono's term of office," Ranariddh wrote, with the word "new" written in boldface.
Annan on April 14 extended the office of his special representative by six months, but has yet to confirm that Widyono would continue on as the world body's representative.
"That is up to the secretary general to decide," Widyono told Reuters in an interview.
Analysts said Ranariddh's letter was likely to put the United Nations in a difficult position as any decision might give the appearance that it was taking sides.

A U.N. official told Reuters that U.N. Assistant Secretary General for Political Affairs Alvaro de Soto will arrive in Phnom Penh on May 3 for discussions with Ranariddh, Hun Sen and Foreign Minister Ung Huot. The issue of Widyono's post would very likely be discussed, the official said.

Relations between Ranariddh and Hun Sen, who formed an uneasy coalition following U.N.-sponsored elections in 1993, have hit a nadir with a deadly grenade attack on an opposition rally last month and a split within Ranariddh's party that the prince blames on Hun Sen.
Ranariddh referred to the grenade attack in his letter and said violence, human rights violations and political intimidation were worsening in Cambodia.
In a second letter to Annan, Ranariddh also bemoaned rising drug trafficking and asked for U.N. financial and technical support to fight the problem.

The Australian and Canadian missions in Phnom Penh issued an advisory on Tuesday advising their citizens to take care when out at night, to stock up on food and water and to steer clear of crowded places and avoid offices of political parties and leaders.
